explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. The angel says, “…The Lord, the God of the spirits of the prophets, has sent His angel to show His servants what must soon take place.” So the One behind this whole vision is the Lord Himself. And look who it's for: His servants.

Not this time, friend, though I get the second guessing on a last page. The angel really does say it: “…The Lord, the God of the spirits of the prophets, has sent His angel to show His servants what must soon take place.” The vision comes from the Lord and goes to His servants. I second guess my oven timer all the time, so I'm in no position to judge.

explanations.answer: Whoever keeps the words of this book
explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. Verse 7 says, “Blessed is the one who keeps the words of prophecy in this book.” Keeping is the word, not just glancing at it once. I own recipe cards I've never kept, so I know the difference.

explanations.answer: Whoever sees an angel up close
explanations.explanation: John did see an angel up close, and he even ended up at his feet (Revelation 22:8). But the blessing in verse 7 isn't handed out for that. It goes to the one who keeps the words of prophecy in this book. Front row seat or not, keeping is what gets named.

Gates do show up in this passage, in verse 14, but nobody is called a gate guard anywhere here. The blessing in verse 7 is for “the one who keeps the words of prophecy in this book.” That's a whole different job description. Good guess on the gates though, friend.

Yes, worship. Verse 8 says John “fell down to worship at the feet of the angel who had shown me these things.” That's a big move, and I think John was completely overwhelmed. The next verse is where the angel sets him straight.

Thanking sounds sweet, friend, but that's not the word the text uses. John says he “fell down to worship at the feet of the angel.” Worship is a much bigger thing than a thank you. That's exactly why the angel steps in next.

If this was a greeting, it was the most dramatic hello in history. But the text says John “fell down to worship at the feet of the angel.” Nobody hits the floor for a simple wave. Worship is the word.

Servant is it, baker. The angel says, “I am a fellow servant with you and your brothers the prophets, and with those who keep the words of this book.” Notice that word fellow. He's standing right alongside John, not above him.

A ruler would be an odd thing to claim right after saying “Do not do that!” The angel calls himself a fellow servant with John, the prophets, and those who keep the words of this book. He puts himself on the same side of the counter as everybody else. No throne in sight.

A judge sits over people, and the angel is doing the opposite here. He says, “I am a fellow servant with you and your brothers the prophets…” Fellow means next to, friend. He's lining himself up with John and the others.

Right, and the angel says it in just two words: “Worship God!” John had the right idea of worshiping, just the wrong direction. The angel points him straight up to the One who deserves it. A good messenger sends the attention to the One who sent him.

The angel actually calls himself a fellow servant with “your brothers the prophets.” So the prophets are on the same team as John and the angel, not the ones to worship. The angel answers with “Worship God!” Friend, that's the only name on his list.
The elders don't show up anywhere in this passage, friend. The angel's whole answer is “Worship God!” He doesn't hand John a list of options. He gives him one.
It's the opposite, friend. The angel says, “Do not seal up the words of prophecy in this book, because the time is near.” Near, not far off. That's the reason he gives for leaving it open.

Right, it's false. The angel says, “Do not seal up the words of prophecy in this book, because the time is near.” A sealed cookie box keeps the cookies safe, but this book is not meant to be shut up. Near is the word.

True. The angel says, “…let the righteous continue to practice righteousness, and the holy continue to be holy.” The verse has two sides, and this is the second half. It's a heavy verse, but it doesn't stop on the heavy part.

It really is there, friend. The angel says, “…let the righteous continue to practice righteousness, and the holy continue to be holy.” That follows the line about the unrighteous and the vile. So the verse has both halves, and this is the one we hold on to.

explanations.answer: By what each one has done
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The verse says, “…My reward is with Me, to give to each one according to what he has done.” Each one, not just a few. That's how it is measured.

explanations.answer: By how long each one waited
explanations.explanation: I know a lot about waiting, friend. I spent years in the back of a junk drawer. But verse 12 doesn't measure the reward by waiting. It says “according to what he has done.”

explanations.answer: By the city each one is from
explanations.explanation: Where anyone is from doesn't come up here at all. Verse 12 says the reward is given “to each one according to what he has done.” No hometown, no zip code. Just what each one has done.

That's it. Verse 14 says those who wash their robes get “the right to the tree of life.” It's a blessing, and the verse names it straight out. The tree of life is also named in the next warning in verse 19.
The golden measuring rod is real, but it's a tool, not a prize. The angel used it to measure the city (Revelation 21:15). In verse 14, what the washed robes get is “the right to the tree of life.”

A crown of twelve stars appears on a woman's head in Revelation 12:1, so it belongs to another scene. Verse 14 here says the ones who wash their robes get “the right to the tree of life.” Tree, not crown. I do like the star idea, though. My sky is full of stars too.
True. Verse 14 says they “may enter the city by its gates.” So it's two gifts in one blessing: the tree of life and the city. Washed robes, open gates.
It's true, friend. Verse 14 says those who wash their robes “may have the right to the tree of life and may enter the city by its gates.” Both are in the same blessing. Gates open for them.

It's the opposite, friend. Verse 15 says, “But outside are the dogs, the sorcerers, the sexually immoral, the murderers, the idolaters, and everyone who loves and practices falsehood.” Outside, not inside. I think this is a heavy verse, so let's just read it plainly.

Right. Verse 15 puts them outside: “But outside are the dogs, the sorcerers, the sexually immoral, the murderers, the idolaters, and everyone who loves and practices falsehood.” That's a heavy verse, and I won't make light of it. It sits right after the blessing for those who enter by the gates.
David, Israel's king, is right. Jesus says, “I am the Root and the Offspring of David…” That ties Him to David's own family line. Two titles, one name.
Saul was an early king of Israel (1 Samuel 11:15), but he isn't the name here. Jesus says, “I am the Root and the Offspring of David…” David, Israel's king, is the one named in the verse.
Herod was a king in Jesus' day (Matthew 2:1), so I see why he came to mind. But Jesus doesn't name him here. He says, “I am the Root and the Offspring of David…” David, Israel's king, is the name.
Yes. The Spirit and the bride say, “Come!” and then comes the open invitation: “Let the one who hears say, ‘Come!’” That could be anyone who hears it, baker. Including you.
Kings don't get a special line in this verse, friend. After the Spirit and the bride, the verse says, “Let the one who hears say, ‘Come!’” It's wide open to whoever hears. No title needed.
No angels at the gates are named in this verse. It says, “Let the one who hears say, ‘Come!’” So the invitation goes to whoever hears. I'm a cookie stamper and even I'm included.

Water, friend. The verse says, “…let the one who is thirsty come, and the one who desires the water of life drink freely.” Thirsty and water go together. And did you catch freely? Nobody is counting cups.
Light sounds beautiful, but it isn't the word in the verse. The text says, “…the one who desires the water of life drink freely.” Drinking goes with water. I see why you went with light, though.

The tree of life shows up in verse 14, but this line is about drinking, and fruit isn't named in it. The verse says, “…the one who desires the water of life drink freely.” Thirsty means water. You're close, just on a different line.

Yes, plagues. Verse 18 says, “If anyone adds to them, God will add to him the plagues described in this book.” It's a serious warning, and I'll leave it as serious. Those are the words, just as they stand.

Visions fit the book, friend, but the warning names something else. Verse 18 says, “…God will add to him the plagues described in this book.” That's a serious verse, so we'll let it stand. Plagues is the word.

Wonders sounds like a nice thing, but this warning isn't nice. Verse 18 says, “…God will add to him the plagues described in this book.” It's a serious line, and we'll treat it that way. Plagues is the word.

True. Verse 19 says, “…God will take away his share in the tree of life and the holy city, which are described in this book.” It's the other half of the warning in verse 18. Serious on both ends, friend.

It is true, friend. Verse 19 says, “…God will take away his share in the tree of life and the holy city, which are described in this book.” It's a serious verse, so I'll keep it simple. It's the partner to the warning about adding in verse 18.
To come. The plea is, “Come, Lord Jesus!” It answers the promise right before it, “Yes, I am coming soon.” That's the whole prayer, and it's short.
Naming the day isn't what the plea asks. It says, “Come, Lord Jesus!” And as for the day, Matthew 24:36 says only the Father knows it. My mustache and I are staying out of that one.
That's the opposite of the plea, friend. It says, “Come, Lord Jesus!” Right before it, He says, “Yes, I am coming soon.” So the ask is for Him to come.
Not John alone, friend. The last verse says, “The grace of the Lord Jesus be with all the saints. Amen.” All the saints. That makes it a much bigger blessing.
False, and I'm glad. The last verse says, “The grace of the Lord Jesus be with all the saints. Amen.” John alone would've made for a very short last line. All the saints is a much bigger table.
